checkpoints.title: Tradeoff duel
checkpoints.prompt: Mobile events arrive up to 2 minutes late. Hourly totals must reflect when each event occurred. Which time model should the job use?

options.label: Processing-time arrival windows
options.sub: bucket each event when Flink receives it
options.verdict: Arrival time is nondeterministic. A delayed mobile event is assigned to a later hour, and replaying the same Kafka records at a different speed can produce different buckets. That breaks occurrence-time totals.

options.label: Event time with bounded watermarks
options.sub: extract occurrence timestamps and allow 2 minutes of disorder
options.verdict: Event timestamps place records in the hour when they occurred. A two-minute bounded-out-of-orderness watermark gives expected delayed records time to arrive, with an explicit tradeoff: windows finalize later for better completeness, while records beyond the bound need a late-event policy.

defend.prompt: Defend the event-time design. Which claims are required?

options.label: Extract the true occurrence timestamp from each event
Set the disorder bound from observed arrival delay
Define a policy for events that arrive after the watermark
A watermark proves every earlier event will eventually arrive

defend.explain: A watermark is the job's progress claim about event time, not proof that every earlier event has arrived or ever will. Timestamp extraction and the disorder bound determine window assignment and finalization latency. Events arriving after that boundary must be dropped, sent to a late-data side output, or included through allowed lateness; durable raw events can also feed an offline reconciliation job that repairs final hourly totals.

checkpoints.title: Streaming ladder
checkpoints.prompt: Reason through event-time progress, overlapping windows, and recovery boundaries.

rungs.q: A two-input operator receives watermarks 12:08 and 12:11. What watermark can it emit downstream?
rungs.note: An operator cannot claim progress beyond its slowest input, so the downstream watermark is the minimum, 12:08.

rungs.q: How many overlapping 5-minute sliding windows contain one event when a new window starts every minute?
rungs.note: A 5-minute window with a 1-minute slide places an event into five concurrent windows, increasing state and computation relative to a tumbling window.

rungs.q: A checkpointed operator calls a plain HTTP endpoint, then fails before the next completed checkpoint. What protects the replayed call?
choices: An idempotency key or transactional protocol
rungs.note: Recovery restores checkpointed Flink state and replays source records, but it cannot roll back an HTTP side effect that already escaped the job.

checkpoints.explain: Watermarks track event-time progress and a multi-input operator is held to its minimum input watermark. Sliding windows trade more frequent results for overlapping state: a 5-minute size and 1-minute slide maintain five memberships per event. Checkpoints consistently restore managed state and source positions, but the guarantee ends at an uncoordinated external side effect, so a plain HTTP sink still needs idempotency or a transactional boundary.

checkpoints.title: Architecture builder
checkpoints.prompt: Build a replay-safe event-time aggregation path from Kafka to an external result.
checkpoints.explain: Records flow from the Kafka source through timestamp and watermark assignment, keyBy partitioning, the checkpointed stateful window, and its window result before reaching the sink. Separately, checkpoint barriers snapshot managed window state and Kafka source positions so recovery can restore state, rewind the source, and replay retained records. Because records after the restored checkpoint can run again, the sink must make repeated writes harmless or coordinate them transactionally. A processing clock mis-buckets delayed events, a local variable is not restored or rescaled, and a fire-and-forget API can duplicate effects after replay.

checkpoints.title: Spot the bottleneck
checkpoints.prompt: Windows stop closing after traffic on one Kafka partition drops to zero, while that partition's broker lag remains zero. Which signal identifies the cause?
checkpoints.explain: An operator advances event time using the minimum watermark across its active inputs. Kafka Partition 3 has zero records per second and zero broker lag, which identifies a legitimately idle input rather than a processing backlog. With source idleness detection disabled, that quiet input remains in the minimum-watermark calculation and holds windows open. Configure idleness detection so Flink excludes the idle input from that minimum until records resume.

wrong.Watermark Progress: The minimum watermark being 18 minutes behind is the symptom that explains why windows remain open, but it does not explain why progress stopped. Disabled source idleness detection is the root configuration error.
wrong.Kafka Partition 3: Zero records per second with zero broker lag proves this partition is legitimately idle, not backlogged or unable to process available records. The source must recognize that state rather than treating the partition itself as faulty.
wrong.Sink: The sink is healthy at 24ms p99 and cannot prevent upstream event-time windows from firing. Window closure is blocked before a result reaches the sink.
